content: 1. For adults, adolescents, and children, antiviral therapies should be selected based on specific clinical scenarios. For adolescent pregnant girls, refer to Chapter 6 for guidance on preventing mother-to-child transmission of HBV using antiviral prophylaxis. For HBV DNA testing, refer to Chapter 9. 2. In cases of treatment failure due to confirmed or suspected antiviral resistance to lamivudine, entecavir, adefovir, or telbivudine, switching to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) is recommended. Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) may be considered as an alternative if available. This recommendation is strong but based on low-certainty evidence. 3. Treatment adherence should be reinforced for all individuals with confirmed or suspected antiviral resistance. In some settings, healthcare providers may consider switching patients to TDF or TAF (if available) from regimens with a low barrier to resistance, even before evidence of treatment failure. However, no formal recommendations are made for this approach. 4. To date, there are only isolated reports of resistance to TDF or TAF when used for hepatitis B treatment. If there is primary non-response to therapy, adherence should be reinforced and monitored. There is no current indication to switch to an alternative drug regimen in such cases. 5. HBV DNA testing is recommended following a positive HBsAg serological test to assess viral load levels for treatment eligibility and to monitor treatment response. Laboratory-based HBV DNA nucleic acid testing (NAT) is the preferred strategy. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 6. Point-of-care (POC) HBV DNA assays may be used as an alternative to laboratory-based testing for assessing HBV DNA levels and monitoring treatment response. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. Assays should meet minimum quality, safety, and performance standards. 7. Reflex HBV DNA testing may be used as an additional strategy to promote linkage to care and treatment. This can be achieved through laboratory-based reflex testing using stored samples or clinic-based reflex testing with immediate sample collection following a positive HBsAg rapid diagnostic test (RDT). This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 8. For individuals with chronic hepatitis B (CHB), serological testing for anti-HDV antibodies is recommended for all HBsAg-positive individuals to improve access to HDV diagnosis and care. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. 9. In settings where universal anti-HDV antibody testing is not feasible, testing may be prioritized for specific populations, such as those born in HDV-endemic regions, individuals with advanced liver disease, those receiving HBV treatment, and individuals with clinical features suggestive of HDV infection (e.g., low HBV DNA with high ALT levels). Other high-risk groups include hemodialysis recipients, people living with hepatitis C or HIV, people who inject drugs, sex workers, and men who have sex with men. 10. For diagnosing hepatitis D in individuals with CHB, a serological assay to detect total anti-HDV should be followed by NAT to detect HDV RNA and confirm active infection. NAT assays should align with WHO HDV RNA standards and report results in IU/mL, with a detection limit of 100 IU/mL or better. 11. Reflex testing for anti-HDV antibodies following a positive HBsAg test and HDV RNA testing (if available) following a positive anti-HDV antibody test may be used as an additional strategy to promote diagnosis. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 12. Treatment adherence should be monitored regularly and at each visit. More frequent monitoring (every 3–6 months during the first year) may be performed for individuals with advanced liver disease, those with adherence concerns, HIV co-infection, or renal impairment. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 13. For individuals not yet receiving treatment, annual monitoring for disease progression, ALT levels, and HBV DNA levels (if available) is recommended. ALT levels fluctuate in CHB, requiring longitudinal monitoring to determine trends. The upper limit of normal (ULN) for ALT is defined as <30 U/L for males and <19 U/L for females. 14. For individuals receiving treatment, monitoring for HBsAg loss, seroreversion to HBsAg positivity after discontinuing treatment, and quantitative HBsAg levels (if available) is recommended. Monitoring HBeAg and anti-HBe is primarily relevant for those initially HBeAg-positive. 15. Decompensated cirrhosis is defined by the development of portal hypertension (ascites, variceal hemorrhage, hepatic encephalopathy), coagulopathy, or liver insufficiency (jaundice). Other features of advanced liver disease or cirrhosis may include hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, pruritus, fatigue, arthralgia, palmar erythema, and edema. 16. Before initiating antiviral therapy, baseline renal function should be assessed, including serum creatinine levels and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). Long-term monitoring of renal function is recommended for individuals on tenofovir disoproxil fumarate therapy, especially in children. 17. Routine surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with abdominal ultrasound and alpha-fetoprotein testing every six months is recommended for individuals with cirrhosis, those with a family history of HCC, and individuals older than 40 years with HBV DNA levels >20,000 IU/mL (if testing is available). 18. Lifelong nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy is recommended for all individuals with cirrhosis due to the risk of reactivation and acute hepatitis flare. Discontinuation of therapy may be considered in exceptional cases for individuals without cirrhosis, with evidence of HBeAg loss and seroconversion to anti-HBe, and with persistently normal ALT and undetectable HBV DNA levels. 19. Retreatment is recommended if there are consistent signs of reactivation, such as HBsAg or HBeAg positivity, increased ALT levels, or detectable HBV DNA (if testing is available).
